corrections.notes: No guideline sets an 18-month minimum. GiACTA treated for 52 weeks, and NICE TA518 limits tocilizumab to 1 year, so 12 months (C) is the evidence-based answer.
corrections.source: GiACTA trial (Stone et al, NEJM 2017); NICE TA518 Tocilizumab for treating giant cell arteritis (2018)
corrections.newExplanation: In the GiACTA trial, tocilizumab combined with a 26-week prednisone taper was given for 52 weeks and achieved higher sustained remission than prednisone alone. NICE TA518 recommends tocilizumab for up to 1 year of uninterrupted treatment. No guideline sets an 18-month minimum, so 12 months is the evidence-based duration. Longer use is individualised, for example for relapse. Source: GiACTA trial (Stone et al, NEJM 2017); NICE TA518 Tocilizumab for treating giant cell arteritis (2018)

corrections.notes: Superseded. CDC 2021 recommends ceftriaxone 500 mg IM alone for uncomplicated gonorrhoea (1 g if >=150 kg), adding doxycycline only if chlamydia isn't excluded. Dual therapy with azithromycin is no longer recommended.
corrections.source: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (Workowski et al, MMWR 2021;70(4)); BASHH UK national guideline for the management of gonorrhoea in adults (2019)
corrections.newExplanation: Uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea is now treated with ceftriaxone monotherapy: 500 mg IM as a single dose in the USA (1 g if 150 kg or more), or 1 g IM in UK BASHH guidance. Routine dual therapy with azithromycin has been dropped because of antimicrobial stewardship and rising azithromycin resistance. If chlamydia hasn't been excluded, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is added. Source: CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines 2021 (Workowski et al, MMWR 2021;70(4)); BASHH UK national guideline for the management of gonorrhoea in adults (2019)

corrections.notes: Superseded. ESC/ERS 2022 recommends initial triple combination including IV/SC prostacyclin for high-risk PAH (WHO FC IV with right heart failure). The keyed prostanoid monotherapy reflects an older expert survey.
corrections.source: 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension (Humbert et al, Eur Heart J 2022)
corrections.newExplanation: This patient has high-risk PAH: WHO functional class IV with right heart failure and markedly raised PVR. ESC/ERS 2022 recommends initial triple combination therapy including an IV or SC prostacyclin analogue, together with an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE5 inhibitor, plus early referral for lung transplant assessment. Monotherapy, including prostanoid monotherapy, is no longer recommended for high-risk patients. Source: 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension (Humbert et al, Eur Heart J 2022)

corrections.notes: In severe haemophilia with suspected head bleeding, factor VIII replacement must be given immediately, before imaging (WFH 2020). Delaying for CT is a recognised error.
corrections.source: WFH Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia, 3rd edition (Srivastava et al, Haemophilia 2020)
corrections.newExplanation: In severe haemophilia A (factor VIII <1%) with suspected head or significant bleeding, factor VIII concentrate should be given immediately, aiming for 80-100% activity. Treatment must not wait for imaging or other investigations. Imaging such as CT, plus haematology input, follow once replacement has started. Delaying factor replacement for a scan is a recognised and potentially fatal error. Source: WFH Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia, 3rd edition (Srivastava et al, Haemophilia 2020)

corrections.notes: T2N1M0 laryngeal SCC is stage III (locoregionally advanced), not localised. Combined modality such as concurrent chemoradiation is indicated, and single-modality surgery or RT is for T1-2N0.
corrections.source: NCCN Guidelines: Head and Neck Cancers; AJCC Cancer Staging Manual, 8th edition
corrections.newExplanation: T2N1M0 squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx is stage III, locoregionally advanced disease. In a fit patient who wants larynx preservation, concurrent chemoradiation with cisplatin is a standard initial approach. Total laryngectomy with neck dissection is the alternative for selected cases. Single-modality surgery or radiotherapy is reserved for early-stage (T1-2N0) laryngeal cancer. Source: NCCN Guidelines: Head and Neck Cancers; AJCC Cancer Staging Manual, 8th edition

corrections.notes: The keyed option (a platelet count on post-operative day 1) is impossible on day 3. A modest fall by day 3 after surgery is expected, and BSH advises continuing LMWH with platelet monitoring every 2-3 days from day 4 to 14.
corrections.source: BCSH guidelines on the diagnosis and management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, 2nd edition (Watson et al, Br J Haematol 2012)
corrections.newExplanation: A modest platelet fall in the first few days after major surgery is expected from haemodilution and consumption. HIT typically causes a fall of more than 50% starting 5-10 days after heparin begins. Here the count is still normal on day 3, so LMWH should continue with ongoing platelet monitoring. BSH advises counts every 2-3 days from day 4 to day 14 in post-operative patients on LMWH, and a 4Ts assessment if the count falls further. Source: BCSH guidelines on the diagnosis and management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, 2nd edition (Watson et al, Br J Haematol 2012)

corrections.notes: Recent heparin exposure without HIT doesn't require a non-heparin anticoagulant. BSH/ACCP advise heparin with baseline and 24-hour platelet counts, and bivalirudin is reserved for suspected or confirmed HIT.
corrections.source: BCSH guidelines on HIT (Watson et al, Br J Haematol 2012); ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy guidelines: HIT (Linkins et al, Chest 2012)
corrections.newExplanation: Previous heparin exposure without HIT doesn't preclude heparin. If exposure was within the last 100 days, circulating antibodies could cause rapid-onset HIT. Guidelines therefore advise a baseline platelet count and a repeat count 24 hours after starting heparin. Non-heparin anticoagulants such as bivalirudin are reserved for suspected or confirmed HIT. Source: BCSH guidelines on HIT (Watson et al, Br J Haematol 2012); ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy guidelines: HIT (Linkins et al, Chest 2012)

corrections.notes: HBV/HCV co-infection is itself a WHO 2024 treatment criterion, and WHO 2024 uses >2000 IU/mL (not 20,000). HBsAg-positive patients starting DAAs need HBV antiviral therapy or prophylaxis because of the reactivation risk (FDA boxed warning).
corrections.source: WHO Guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, care and treatment of people with chronic hepatitis B infection (2024); AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance; FDA Drug Safety Communication on HBV reactivation with DAAs (2016)
corrections.newExplanation: HBV can reactivate when HCV is cleared with direct-acting antivirals. HBsAg-positive patients who meet HBV treatment criteria should start nucleos(t)ide therapy before or with the DAAs. Here HBV DNA is above 2,000 IU/mL, the WHO 2024 threshold, and HBV/HCV co-infection is itself a WHO 2024 treatment criterion. Tenofovir or entecavir alongside the DAAs is appropriate. Source: WHO Guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, care and treatment of people with chronic hepatitis B infection (2024); AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance; FDA Drug Safety Communication on HBV reactivation with DAAs (2016)

corrections.notes: For treatment-naive GT1b with compensated cirrhosis, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks is a recommended regimen (EXPEDITION-8). Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir is reserved for DAA-experienced patients, and the stem doesn't state prior treatment.
corrections.source: EASL Recommendations on Treatment of Hepatitis C, final update 2020; AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance; EXPEDITION-8 (Brown et al, J Hepatol 2020)
corrections.newExplanation: For treatment-naive genotype 1b HCV with compensated cirrhosis, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks is recommended, supported by the EXPEDITION-8 trial with SVR12 above 97%. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks is an alternative. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir is reserved for DAA-experienced patients, and the 8-week ledipasvir/sofosbuvir course isn't recommended in cirrhosis. Source: EASL Recommendations on Treatment of Hepatitis C, final update 2020; AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance; EXPEDITION-8 (Brown et al, J Hepatol 2020)

corrections.notes: The ERS/ILTS HPS oxygenation criterion is an A-a gradient >=15 mmHg (>=20 if over 64) or PaO2 <80 mmHg. That matches B, not the keyed 'PaO2 <70 and A-a >20'.
corrections.source: ILTS Practice Guidelines: Hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension (Krowka et al, Transplantation 2016); ERS Task Force on pulmonary-hepatic vascular disorders (Rodriguez-Roisin et al, Eur Respir J 2004)
corrections.newExplanation: HPS requires liver disease or portal hypertension, intrapulmonary vascular dilatation on contrast echocardiography, and impaired oxygenation. The oxygenation criterion is an A-a gradient of at least 15 mmHg (at least 20 mmHg if over 64) or PaO2 below 80 mmHg on room air. A normal A-a gradient below 15 mmHg in this 48-year-old would rule out HPS. Severity is then graded by PaO2. Source: ILTS Practice Guidelines: Hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension (Krowka et al, Transplantation 2016); ERS Task Force on pulmonary-hepatic vascular disorders (Rodriguez-Roisin et al, Eur Respir J 2004)

corrections.notes: The 'HRS type 2' terminology is superseded. ICA/ADQI now classify this as HRS-NAKI (HRS-AKD or HRS-CKD), so the keyed option should be relabelled.
corrections.source: ICA-ADQI consensus on acute kidney injury in cirrhosis (Nadim et al, J Hepatol 2024); Angeli et al, News in pathophysiology, definition and classification of HRS (J Hepatol 2019)
corrections.newExplanation: A gradual creatinine rise over weeks in cirrhosis with ascites, low urine sodium, no shock, infection or nephrotoxins, and no response to stopping diuretics fits functional hepatorenal physiology with a subacute course. This was formerly called HRS type 2. Current ICA/ADQI terminology classifies it as HRS-NAKI: HRS-AKD if under 3 months, or HRS-CKD if longer. HRS-AKI, formerly type 1, is a rapid rise meeting AKI criteria. Source: ICA-ADQI consensus on acute kidney injury in cirrhosis (Nadim et al, J Hepatol 2024); Angeli et al, News in pathophysiology, definition and classification of HRS (J Hepatol 2019)

optionEdits.after: Hepatorenal syndrome-non-AKI (HRS-NAKI; HRS-AKD/HRS-CKD), formerly HRS type 2.

corrections.notes: Standard monitoring during adjuvant trastuzumab is LVEF assessment at baseline and every 3 months during treatment (ESMO, ESC cardio-oncology, product labelling), not annually.
corrections.source: ESC 2022 Guidelines on cardio-oncology (Lyon et al, Eur Heart J 2022); ESMO consensus recommendations on cardiac toxicity (Curigliano et al, Ann Oncol 2020)
corrections.newExplanation: Trastuzumab can cause left ventricular dysfunction, which is usually reversible if detected early. Guidelines recommend LVEF assessment by echocardiography or MUGA at baseline and every 3 months during adjuvant trastuzumab, plus at completion and when symptoms develop. Annual monitoring during treatment is too infrequent. Treatment is held if LVEF falls significantly, for example by 10 or more points to below 50%. Source: ESC 2022 Guidelines on cardio-oncology (Lyon et al, Eur Heart J 2022); ESMO consensus recommendations on cardiac toxicity (Curigliano et al, Ann Oncol 2020)

corrections.notes: BAD 2018 makes a 12-week tetracycline course first-line for mild-moderate HS and clindamycin-rifampicin second-line. The cited NICE NG73 is the endometriosis guideline, not HS.
corrections.source: British Association of Dermatologists guidelines for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa 2018 (Ingram et al, Br J Dermatol 2019); European S2k guideline for HS (Zouboulis et al, JEADV 2024)
corrections.newExplanation: BAD guidance recommends a 12-week course of an oral tetracycline, such as doxycycline 100 mg daily or lymecycline 408 mg daily, as first-line systemic treatment for mild to moderate HS. Clindamycin 300 mg plus rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10-12 weeks is second-line, or used for more severe disease. Adalimumab is considered if conventional systemic therapy fails. Source: British Association of Dermatologists guidelines for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa 2018 (Ingram et al, Br J Dermatol 2019); European S2k guideline for HS (Zouboulis et al, JEADV 2024)
